The Eclectus parrot (Eclectus roratus) exhibits a striking pattern of sexual dimorphism that extends well beyond plumage coloration into key life-history traits. Field studies on the Cape York Peninsula indicate that newly laid eggs weigh approximately 21 grams [Ww0 = approximately 21 grams], a modest investment given the species' considerable size. Hatchlings emerge from the incubated egg at a wet birth mass of about 17 grams [Wwb = about 17 grams], reflecting the limited yolk reserves available to the altricial neonate. Incubation at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] requires approximately 28 days [ab = approximately 28 days], a duration that aligns with the extended developmental periods typical of large parrots. The initial fragility of the chick, weighing roughly 17 grams at hatching, underscores the critical role of biparental provisioning during the first weeks of life.

During the early postnatal period, the developing chick undergoes rapid somatic growth under the consistent thermal conditions of the nest cavity. Under the prevailing temperatures of approximately 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], the nestling reaches the crucial developmental milestone of fledging at 84 days after hatching [tx = 84 days after hatching]. This interval, which encompasses feather development and wing muscle strengthening, is slightly protracted compared to smaller Psittaciformes, likely reflecting the energetic demands of attaining a large body size. The downy chick, initially weighing only about 17 grams, transforms into a fully feathered fledgling capable of short flights by the time it leaves the cavity. The protracted nestling period is thought to reduce predation risk by ensuring that the young bird is well-developed upon its first departure from the nest hollow.

Reproductive senescence and body mass exhibit notable variation between the sexes in Eclectus roratus. While females typically attain an ultimate wet weight of approximately 560.8 grams [Wwi = approximately 560.8 grams], males are slightly heavier on average, reaching an adult body mass of about 561.5 grams [Wwi = about 561.5 grams]. This modest sexual size dimorphism, with males being marginally larger, is unusual among parrots where females are often the heavier sex. Female mass fluctuates significantly during the breeding cycle, increasing prior to egg-laying and declining during incubation and chick-rearing. The maximum recorded longevity for this species under captive conditions, when maintained at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], is approximately 28 years [am = approximately 28 years], a figure that places it among the longer-lived members of the Psittacidae family.

The onset of reproductive maturity follows a clear sequence of developmental events linked to the thermal environment of the tropical lowlands. Puberty, defined by the initiation of gonadal maturation, is reached at 252 days after hatching [tp = 252 days after hatching] under the typical ambient temperatures of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C] found within the nest hollow. This relatively rapid maturation for a parrot of this body size may be an adaptation to unpredictable food resources, allowing young birds to become reproductively viable quickly if conditions permit. However, actual first breeding is typically deferred considerably, with the first successful brood occurring at approximately 730 days after hatching [tR = approximately 730 days after hatching], marking a two-year lag between physiological capability and realize at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]d reproduction. This deferred reproduction is thought to allow young birds to establish territories and acquire the foraging skills necessary to support offspring.

Reproductive output in the Eclectus parrot is constrained by the limited availability of suitable nest hollows and the energetic costs of raising altricial young. Females typically produce one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], laying exactly 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 eggs per clutch]. This single annual cycle, combined with the relatively small clutch size, results in a low annual reproductive rate, a common pattern among large, long-lived parrots that invest heavily in each offspring. The extended period of parental care, from incubation through to post-fledging provisioning, further limits the potential for multiple broods. This conservative reproductive strategy, trade-off with high adult survival, allows the species to persist in the face of variable resource availability across its range.
